title: What It Actually Costs — Module Quiz

items.q: When a provider charges per token, one token is:
options: One word
A chunk roughly three-quarters of an English word
A single character
items.explain: Common words are one token; longer or unusual ones split. About 100 tokens to 75 English words.

items.q: The same meaning written in Hindi rather than English usually costs:
options: The same, since the meaning is identical
Several times more tokens
Fewer tokens, as the script is denser
items.explain: Tokenisers were built largely on English, so other scripts split into many more tokens — you pay more and hit limits sooner.

items.q: Why does message forty in a thread cost more than message one?
options: Providers raise prices during long sessions
The whole conversation is re-sent each time, so the context keeps growing
Later answers are always longer
items.explain: Models have no memory between calls, so the history travels with every new message.

items.q: Between input and output tokens:
options: Input is usually the more expensive
Output is usually the more expensive, often several times
They are always priced identically
items.explain: That makes 'answer in one paragraph' a genuine saving rather than only a readability preference.

items.q: The most common cause of quietly rising cost:
options: Using a more capable model
Long conversations, since the whole history is re-sent each turn
Asking more questions per day
items.explain: Cost per message climbs even though your questions stay the same size — and long threads follow instructions worse too.

items.q: A prompt that routinely needs four attempts costs:
options: The same as one, since only the final answer counts
Four times — discarded attempts are billed identically
Less, because failed runs are free
items.explain: An evaluation set pays for itself here: a prompt that works first time is a cost improvement as well as a quality one.

items.q: Which change improves cost and answer quality together?
options: Attaching only the section the task needs
Using a larger model
Requesting longer answers
items.explain: Relevant material is not diluted and there is less chance of drawing on the wrong part.

items.q: Which task most needs the most capable model?
options: Extracting a date from an email
A multi-step problem where getting step two wrong ruins the rest
Reformatting a list into a table
items.explain: Dependent steps, fine judgement, long inputs and expensive errors are where capability earns its price.

items.q: The right way to decide which model a task needs:
options: Use the most capable to be safe
Run your evaluation set against the cheaper model and compare
Follow the provider's recommendation
items.explain: The answer is task-specific and often surprising; fifteen minutes of measurement can remove most of a workflow's cost.

items.q: The two-tier pattern means:
options: Alternating between two providers
Cheap model first, escalating only flagged uncertain cases
Paying for two subscriptions
items.explain: If most cases are routine, you pay the premium only on the minority.

items.q: The total cost of an AI task is:
options: The subscription divided across your tasks
Money plus prompting, verification and correction time
The per-token charge for the request
items.explain: Only one of the four terms arrives as an invoice, which is why the arithmetic gets skipped.

items.q: Why do people misjudge tasks that are actually losses?
options: The output appears instantly, and the checking afterwards does not feel like part of it
Billing is delayed
They chose the wrong model
items.explain: The feeling of efficiency comes from response speed. The forty minutes afterwards are still part of the cost.

items.q: Comparing a free tier to a paid one fairly means comparing:
options: Zero against the monthly fee
The fee against the time the free tier's friction costs you
The feature lists
items.explain: Free costs queue time, lower limits and workarounds. Put time on both sides.

items.q: Free tiers usually limit you by:
options: Removing all capability
Message caps, smaller models after the cap, and queueing
Restricting which languages you may use
items.explain: The everyday work in E3, E4 and E5 is generally within reach; volume and extras are what you give up.

items.q: The strongest reason to run a model on your own machine:
options: It is more capable than hosted models
Privacy — nothing leaves your device, which changes what you may put in
It is faster
items.explain: For confidential material or a policy forbidding external services, it is frequently the only compliant option.

items.q: Buying more powerful hardware to avoid a subscription is:
options: Usually sound, since hardware lasts
Usually false economy
Required for any local model
items.explain: Count the total cost including your time maintaining it, not only the avoided fee.

items.q: The advertised subscription price is best treated as:
options: The final cost
A floor, before conversion fees, card charges and tax
An estimate that usually falls
items.explain: Currency markups, bank charges and checkout tax stack on top, and cards are sometimes declined outright.

items.q: Misrepresenting your country to obtain regional pricing risks:
options: A warning email
Losing the account entirely, including anything stored in it
Nothing, since providers rarely check
items.explain: The risk is asymmetric — a modest saving staked against an account you may depend on.

items.q: For work in a local language, a regional provider may be:
options: Always worse than a global one
Sometimes better, since region-specific models can outperform general ones
Identical, as they use the same models
items.explain: Local currency, local payment methods and better language coverage can coincide.

items.q: A spending cap should be set:
options: Once you understand your typical usage
Before anything runs unattended
Only for API access, not subscriptions
items.explain: Runaway cases happen in minutes. A cap added afterwards is a lesson rather than a safeguard.

items.q: Which pattern most commonly causes a runaway cost?
options: A person asking many questions in a day
An unbounded retry loop, or a trigger firing on its own output
Using the most capable model
items.explain: The runaway shapes share one property: nothing in the design says how many times it can run.

items.q: The question to answer before any unattended automation goes live:
options: How accurate is the output?
What is the maximum number of times this can run in an hour, and what does that cost?
Which model should it use?
items.explain: If you cannot answer it, the design is not finished. If the answer is 'unlimited', add a limit.

items.q: The counterfactual question is:
options: Did this help?
What would have happened without it?
How often do I use it?
items.explain: Everything helps a little. Only the comparison against not using it measures anything.

items.q: Having already paid for a year should affect whether you keep using it:
options: Yes — you should get value from what you paid
No — the money is gone either way; only next month is the question
Only if the tool has improved since
items.explain: That is the sunk-cost trap, and it leads to using a tool where it does not help because stopping feels wasteful.
